content: I would like to bring to everyone's attention that @Andrew Yang and I and separately @ooovi and @Martin Winter have been working on the long-awaited convexity refactor. Here are the relevant PRs:
#37592 indexed convex combinations
#38905 convex sets in a convex space
#38934 convex hull in a convex space
I have more ready-to-be-PRed material on my fork: product of convex spaces, convex/concave functions
Martin and Olivia have independently been developing convexity in an affine space. This is necessary and isn't blocking my work but will take some thought to be laid over it

Thanks for your work! I am delighted these PRs exist. While there is similar work in our repo, it has not yet reached this level. Instead we can contribute

  • an abstract AffineSpace which is an analogue of ConvexSpace but with a notion of affine combination.
  • a bundled ConvexSet which will be the ananlogue of convex cone (currently still named PointedCone) on the affine side.
  • IsFaceOf for ConvexSet as an affine equivalent of the face PR #33664.
  • Polytope as an affine equivalent of FG cone.
  • AffineHomogenization as the way to translate between the linear and affine settings
I think we should discuss how these contributions fit into the refactor. And ideally we should use your PRs to build our stuff on top.

Most relevant for now, perhaps, are the abstract affine spaces: I think they should live in between ConvexSpace and AddTorsor. I would like to hear your opinion on:

  1. should we plan with them in mind right now? I don't have any particular application for them. But neither do I have any for ConvexSpace. They just appeared to me as a very natural intermediate step.
  2. if we want to have them, does this have any consequences for the current PRs?

1. Andrew and I do have an application for ConvexSpace: We need to take combinations of points inside a standard simplex. If you do not have an application for AffineSpace, we could revisit it later
  2. No, we will want the current PRs regardless because they work in more generality than everything you have been considering so far

We need to take combinations of points inside a standard simplex.

I don't understand this application. Is this not just in usual affine space?

Yes, this embeds in the usual affine space, but they want that the barycenters are directly elements in the standard simplex, rather than points in the affine space which happen to belong to the standard simplex. For certain practical purposes, it makes a significant difference.
I am curious about this new definition of AffineSpace. Is it equivalent to the AddTorsor definition or will be more general?

Weiyi Wang said:

I am curious about this new definition of AffineSpace. Is it equivalent to the AddTorsor definition or will be more general?

It is almost verbatim the definition of ConvexSpace except that StdSimplex does not require non-negative weights (and should not be called StdSimplex).

I am almost sure that this is more general than AddTorsor, but I have no example.

Joël Riou said:

Yes, this embeds in the usual affine space, but they want that the barycenters are directly elements in the standard simplex, rather than points in the affine space which happen to belong to the standard simplex. For certain practical purposes, it makes a significant difference.

I agree, and in retrospect, I have non-geometric examples in mind as well. For examples lattices (in the sense of order theory).

#39205 ConvexSet, the bundled version of IsConvexSet

Reading #38934, I wonder whether convexHull should generate a bundled ConvexSet rather than a plain Set. This would be analogous to how PointedCone.hull generates a PointedCone rather than just a set (or SubMulAction) in the shape of a convex cone.
What do you need bundled convex sets for?

Someday someone will need it for convex geometry, Minkowski sums etc. Right now, it is the object on which we plan to build the affine IsFaceOf (makes no sense for general sets).

Also we will need Polytopes as bundled objects and I am pondering whether they should extend ConvexSet in the same way as PolyhedralCone will extend PointedCone.
Can we avoid introducing it until an application arises?
This means we would need to build IsFaceOf on sets ... I am skeptical

Maybe this counts as an application: we built homogenization to construct an order isomorphism between convex cones and convex sets, and between their respective face lattices. This is only possible if we have ConvexSet to define the lattice of convex sets.

Martin Winter said:

This means we would need to build IsFaceOf on sets ... I am skeptical

Isn't this a good idea anyway, to avoid having to do it separately for convex cones and convex sets?
But their notions of faces are different. For one of them a face can be empty, for the other one not.
Isn't a face in a convex cone just a face (in the set sense) that contains the lineality space of the cone?
Yes.

Yaël Dillies said:

Martin Winter said:

This means we would need to build IsFaceOf on sets ... I am skeptical

Isn't this a good idea anyway, to avoid having to do it separately for convex cones and convex sets?

Regarding this: convex cones are still convex sets, so I don' see why this would be an argument for doing it on Set.

Yaël Dillies said:

#38905 convex sets in a convex space

Ready for review
#39407 product of convex spaces

Some thoughts on faces and bundled ConvexSet:

  1. the usual between-ness definition of an extreme point/face for general sets SSS appears pretty detached from what one wants to study here. For example, if SSS is finite with points in general position, every point is an extreme point, and every subset is an extreme face. This might be interesting in synthetic geometry where one studies an abstract notion of between-ness, but maybe not under the terms "convexity" and "extreme"?
  2. one can also define a point x∈Sx\in Sx∈S as "extreme" if x∉conv⁡(S∖{x})x\not\in\operatorname{conv}(S\setminus\{x\})x∈conv(S∖{x}). This retreats to convex sets in some sense. The extreme face version seems to be that FFF is an extreme face if F=conv⁡(F)∩SF=\operatorname{conv}(F)\cap SF=conv(F)∩S and conv⁡(F)∩conv⁡(S∖F)=∅\operatorname{conv}(F)\cap\operatorname{conv}(S\setminus F)=\varnothingconv(F)∩conv(S∖F)=∅. Is this better than using the between-ness definition on ConvexSet?
  3. ConvexSet is the substructure notion of ConvexSpace, so a very natural definition. They too have the structure of a convex space. convexHull is their span equivalent, bringing me back to the question whether convexHull should generate a ConvexSet in the first place (like span generates a submodule, not a submodule-shaped set).
  4. Writing point 3 I wondered whether IsFaceOf should be defined on ConvexSpace itself rather than on ConvexSet. I don't know.

Can we please talk about the generality of ConvexSpace?

It happened to me that several definitions of the same concept (for example "being an extreme point" or "being in convex position") become non-equivalent without additional assumptions. Can someone, who pushed for this generality, comment on the below?:

  1. should we use sConvexComb whenever possible instead of convexCombPair? When is it enough to use the pair-version? This comes up when defining extreme points.
  2. should we use Semiring instead of Ring whenever possible. A main drawback of semiring is that from s = 1 and s + t = 1 does not follow t = 0 without further assumptions such as [IsLeftCancelAdd R]. Should we prefer the latter over [Ring R]?
  3. May we assume that the convex space is "cancelative" whenever we need it, i.e., that convexCombPair s t hs ht h x is injective for 0 < t. Or does someone care about a more fine-grained property hierarchy. For example there is also x ≠ y → convexCombPair s t hs ht h x y = x → s = 1 (which is not equivalent to t = 0 unless the ring is left cancelative).

1. Use sConvexComb in general. Convexity properties can be expressed in terms of convexCombPair only over a semifield.
  2. Non-cancellative semirings are probably not worth thinking about.
  3. Sure, why not. When does this show up?

Yaël Dillies said:

  1. Sure, why not. When does this show up?

For example when I want to show that the following three definitions of an extreme point xxx of a convex set AAA are equivalent:

  • A∖{x}A\setminus\{x\}A∖{x} is convex
  • x∉conv⁡(A∖x)x\not\in\operatorname{conv}(A\setminus{x})x∈conv(A∖x)
  • if xxx lies in the convex comb of a set S⊆AS\subseteq AS⊆A, then x∈Sx\in Sx∈S

(actually, I am not sure anymore the above is a correct example)

Or when I want to show that for sets S,TS,TS,T in convex position holds conv⁡(S)=conv⁡(T)↔S=T\operatorname{conv}(S)=\operatorname{conv}(T)\leftrightarrow S=Tconv(S)=conv(T)↔S=T.

One should note that cancelativity is pretty strong. The Stone-Kneser theorem states that cancelative convex spaces are essentially convex sets in affine spaces.

So this is a strong assumption!

Martin Winter said:

  • A∖{x}A \setminus \{x\}A∖{x} is convex
  • x∉conv⁡(A∖x)x\not\in\operatorname{conv}(A\setminus{x})x∈conv(A∖x)
  • if xxx lies in the convex comb of a set S⊆AS\subseteq AS⊆A, then x∈Sx\in Sx∈S

And by the way, the first two definitions make sense for a general closure operator. Does it make sense to define the concept of an extreme point even more abstractly?
Possibly, but this shouldn't come at the cost of usability/discoverability
that last one makes sense too in that setting? if x is in the closure of some set S, then x is in S?
Closure operators aren't necessarily on sets
then how do the first two definitions generalize? non-membership and singletons are not order-theoretic things either?

that last one makes sense too in that setting? if x is in the closure of some set S, then x is in S?

True. This also as a version for closure operators.

I tinkered with the idea of extreme faces for general closure operators. This is what I currently think it should look like:

import Mathlib.Order.Closure

variable {X : Type*} [SemilatticeInf X] {cl : ClosureOperator X}

structure IsExtremeFace (S F : cl.Closeds) where
  le : F ≤ S
  forall_le_closure_inf : ∀ T : X, T ≤ S → cl (T ⊓ F) = cl T ⊓ F

And yes, this only makes sense for closed sets. Otherwise one would need to replace cl in the definition by some relative closure operator S ⊓ cl _.

Lately I am confused about the intended way to use convex spaces in combination with modules and affine spaces.

  • If I want the standard convex space structure on a module, I add
    variable [ConvexSpace R M] [IsModuleConvexSpace R M].

  • If I want the standard convex space structure on an affine space I write
    attribute [local instance] AddTorsor.toConvexSpace
    Problem now is that after this line every module gets automatically inferred a convex space structure by interpreting it as an affine space. How do I get the correct IsModuleConvexSpace now? I think using IsModuleConvexSpace.ofModule causes bad diamonds.

  • How do I express that the convex space structures on an affine space and on the underlying module are compatible? Is there such a way? Should one be derived from the other automatically?

Is there some code that demonstrates the intended use, either in mathlib or elsewhere?

And there is also always the question whether we even ever want a non-standard convex space structure on a module or affine space. That is, whether we cannot just infer the standard one every time.

Here are more concrete questions:

  1. Why do we have ConvexSpace.ofModule but AddTorsor.toConvexSpace?
  2. Why don't we have IsAffineConvexSpace?

1. Why is this not an instance:
attribute [local instance] ConvexSpace.ofModule in
protected lemma IsModuleConvexSpace.ofModule : IsModuleConvexSpace R M where
  sConvexComb_eq_sum _ := rfl

Martin Winter said:

In am aware of this. Yet, many things still compile if I replace Ring by Semiring or AddCommGroup by AddCommMonoid. This might not be true for the parts needed to state IsAffineConvexSpace, but I have not checked this far.

If you have AddTorsor G P with g : G and p : P, then p -ᵥ (g +ᵥ p) = -g, so even if you replace AddGroup with AddMonoid in the definition of AddTorsor it's not mathematically more general.
Not mathematically more general, but then modules that are AddCommMonoids over Semirings could still be affine spaces and one would not need both IsModuleConvexSpace and IsAffineConvexSpace.
modules that are AddCommMonoids over Semirings are not necessarily AddCommGroups, but if we have AddTorsor G P then G must be a Group
for p : P, setting -g := p -ᵥ (g +ᵥ p) we verify the identity -g + g = 0 as (p -ᵥ (g +ᵥ p)) + g = (((p -ᵥ (g +ᵥ p)) + g) +ᵥ p) -ᵥ p = ((p -ᵥ (g +ᵥ p)) +ᵥ (g +ᵥ p)) -ᵥ p = p -ᵥ p = (0 +ᵥ p) -ᵥ p = 0
That sounds convincing. Just feels weird to implement both affine and linear convex structures when they are the same in all cases that I can think of.

I think a lot of things still work for an AddCommGroup that's a module over a Semiring, but it's not clear that the case where you have subtraction in the module but not the scalars is a mathematically useful generalization.
in this case, I think the action of the semiring on the module would factor through its ring of differences
